incidents.title: App servers open a connection per request
incidents.brief: Each HTTP request opens a new Postgres connection and p99 login time on the database climbs.
incidents.constraint: The database max_connections is 200 and there are 40 app pods.
incidents.question: What is the first fix?

choices.label: Bound pool
choices.resultBody: Reuse a bounded connection pool per process instead of connecting per request.

choices.label: Raise max conn
choices.resultBody: Raising max_connections lets more sessions in, but 40 pods still open a fresh TCP, TLS and auth handshake per request; Postgres forks a backend per login and CPU pins at 100%.

choices.label: Connect per request
choices.resultBody: Opening a new connection on every retry doubles the logins Postgres must fork and authenticate, and sessions slam into the 200 max_connections limit within seconds.

hints: Sessions to the database are unbounded.
Handshake cost is the tax.
Reuse a bounded pool.

incidents.title: Postgres refuses logins after payroll scale-out
incidents.brief: Ledgerly's API autoscaled to 50 pods for payroll day. Each pod's pool opens 50 connections, so Postgres sees 2,500 attempts against max_connections 500 and rejects new sessions.
incidents.constraint: Peak load needs only ~300 busy connections, and the 64 GB primary cannot host thousands of backends.
incidents.question: How do you stop scale-out from exhausting the database?

choices.label: Set per-pod pool to max_connections divided by max pods

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Cheap and immediate, but pod count and pool size are now coupled.

choices.resultBody: Pools drop to 8 per pod and HPA max is pinned at 60, so the fleet can never hold more than 480 sessions; peak needs ~300, so p95 falls to 90 ms. Cost: pool size and replica count are now coupled, and every scaling change must redo that division.

choices.label: Raise max_connections to 3,000 on the primary
choices.resultBody: Postgres now accepts all 2,500 sessions, but each is a forked backend with its own memory and snapshot overhead; CPU pins at 99% on context switches and p95 gets worse, reaching 3.1 s.

choices.label: Point half the pods at a new read replica
choices.resultBody: Payroll traffic is 80% writes, so the 25 pods sent to the read-only replica fail their INSERTs and retry against the primary, which still sees 1,250 connection attempts for 500 slots.

hints: Multiply two numbers in the brief and compare the result with a third.
The database limit is fixed; the per-pod pool size is a config value.
Work backwards from max_connections to what each pod may hold at maximum scale.

incidents.title: Flash sale Lambdas can't log in to Postgres
incidents.brief: A TicketDrop flash sale pushes Lambda concurrency from 40 to 900 in one minute. Each execution environment opens its own Postgres connection, and RDS rejects logins past max_connections 400.
incidents.constraint: The sale must stay open: throttling the checkout function is not allowed.
incidents.question: What lets 900 concurrent functions share 400 database connections?

choices.label: Route functions through RDS Proxy's shared connection pool

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Multiplexes many short-lived callers onto a warm pool, for a proxy bill and ~1-2 ms per query.

choices.resultBody: RDS Proxy keeps ~300 warm connections and lends one per transaction, so 900 functions multiplex onto them and the login storm stops. Cost: about 1-2 ms extra per query, a per-vCPU proxy bill, and session state (SET, temp tables) pins a connection and defeats multiplexing.

choices.label: Open a pool of 5 connections inside each function
choices.resultBody: A pool inside a Lambda serves one invocation at a time, so 900 environments now try to hold 4,500 connections against the 400 limit and login failures more than double.

choices.label: Cap checkout at 300 reserved concurrency
choices.resultBody: Postgres recovers, but 600 of 900 concurrent checkouts get TooManyRequestsException during the drop, which the constraint forbids; fans refresh and roughly double inbound traffic.

hints: Count the callers and count the connection slots.
A function instance can't share its connections with its neighbours on its own.
Something long-lived has to own the connections on the functions' behalf.

incidents.title: Checkout threads queue for a DB connection
incidents.brief: Cartwheel runs 6 pods at 600 req/s each. Every request holds a connection for 40 ms, but each pod's pool has 10 connections, and 180 of 200 servlet threads sit blocked waiting.
incidents.constraint: Postgres max_connections is 300, and the database is idling at 45% CPU.
incidents.question: What pool size should each pod run?

choices.label: Size pools from arrival rate times hold time, ~30 each

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Right-sized pool; must be recomputed when traffic or query time changes.

choices.resultBody: Little's law: 600 req/s x 0.04 s = ~24 connections busy per pod, so a pool of 30 leaves headroom and 6 x 30 = 180 stays under 300. Pool waits vanish and p95 drops to 70 ms. Cost: DB CPU rises to ~60%, and the math must be redone when pods or query times change.

choices.label: Match each pool to all 200 servlet threads
choices.resultBody: Six pods x 200 connections asks Postgres for 1,200 sessions; only about 1.5 pods' worth get in, the rest hit 'too many clients', and errors more than triple.

choices.label: Cut servlet threads to 10 to match the pool
choices.resultTitle: Queue moved to the load balancer
choices.resultBody: No thread blocks now, but 10 concurrent requests at 40 ms caps each pod at ~250 req/s against 600 arriving, so the LB queue grows and p95 hits 3 s.

hints: The pool is too small, but by how much?
Connections in use = arrivals per second x seconds each one is held.
Check your number against max_connections divided by the pod count.

incidents.title: Tenants query each other's schemas
incidents.brief: Plotline runs PgBouncer in transaction mode: 1,200 app clients share 100 server connections. Code runs SET search_path once per request, and 3% of queries land in another tenant's schema.
incidents.constraint: Postgres can afford about 100 server connections; session pooling would need 1,200.
incidents.question: How do you stop tenant state leaking across pooled connections?

choices.label: Use SET LOCAL inside each request's explicit transaction

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Keeps 12:1 multiplexing; every request must run in an explicit transaction.

choices.resultBody: SET LOCAL scopes search_path to the transaction PgBouncer lends out, so it resets at COMMIT and can't leak, while 1,200 clients still share 100 server connections. Cost: each request needs BEGIN/COMMIT, and other session features (advisory locks, LISTEN, WITH HOLD cursors) stay off-limits.

choices.label: Switch PgBouncer to session pooling mode
choices.resultBody: Session mode stops the leak but pins one server connection per client for its whole life, so 1,100 clients wait in PgBouncer's queue and p95 jumps from 45 ms to 4 s.

choices.label: Force RESET ALL after every transaction in PgBouncer
choices.resultBody: With server_reset_query_always on, RESET ALL runs between the SET and the next statement, so queries stop leaking but now land in the public schema; 'relation does not exist' errors jump to 3,000/s.

hints: The leak only happens because of the proxy's current mode.
In this mode a server connection belongs to a client for one transaction only.
Make the setting's lifetime match the length of the connection loan.

incidents.title: Pool drains 40 minutes after every restart
incidents.brief: Since Tuesday's deploy, Bookly's 20-connection pool per pod empties about 40 minutes after start. The new card-decline path returns early without releasing its connection, so requests wait 30 s.
incidents.constraint: Postgres shows 20 idle sessions per pod, and restarts only buy another 40 minutes.
incidents.question: What stops connections from disappearing?

choices.label: Release in finally blocks and turn on leak detection

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Fixes the root cause; requires a sweep of every early-return path.

choices.resultBody: try/finally (or a with/using block) returns the connection on the decline path too, and a 10 s leakDetectionThreshold logs the stack of any future borrower that holds on. Usage settles at 6 of 20. Cost: a code sweep of every early return, plus log noise from slow but legitimate queries.

choices.label: Double the pool to 40 connections per pod
choices.resultBody: Latency recovers for now, but the same leak drains 40 connections in about 80 minutes instead of 40, and Postgres carries twice as many orphaned idle sessions per pod.

choices.label: Cut the pool checkout timeout from 30 s to 2 s
choices.resultBody: Requests now fail after 2 s instead of hanging for 30 s, which frees threads, but all 20 connections are still leaked, so nearly every booking still errors.

hints: The connections aren't lost in Postgres; the app still owns them.
Look at the code path that shipped in Tuesday's deploy.
Every borrow needs a return on every exit, including error paths.
